content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a method for video summarization, which takes multiple semantics levels into account, namely, event, shot, and frame. Frames are segmented based on these different granularities, and the segment information is fed into the model to facilitate the importance score prediction. Another point is that the paper tries to evaluate the video summarization performance based on considering the subjectivity of the task. To do this, video clips are sampled from different videos and concatenated based on different criteria. The experimental results show some performance gains compared with reproduced scores of existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

The subjectivity of the video summarization task is an important perspective. I think this cast an inherent question about the validity of using a single set of ground-truth labels for evaluating a video summarization method. 

### Weaknesses:

It is a little bit hard to see what the supervision at higher semantic levels tries to provide. At a higher level, the model tries to predict a score for a semantic unit that is the average of the ground-truth scores within the unit. According to the experimental results, the event-level supervision works well to boost performance, so there should be some bias in the distribution of ground-truth scores. Some examples of such average scores along the time axis will be helpful to see what this supervision actually is. Also, since the supervision signal at a higher semantic level is the same as the frame level, there is no information gain. In this sense, some more explanation about the use of this multi-level supervision is also helpful.

Although the paper tries to raise an interesting question of subjectivity, I don’t see how diversity and importance involve it. According to Section 1, Paragraph 5, diversity seems rather objective (e.g., the semantic features of selected frames should be far from each other), and importance involves a collective opinion of people. I don’t see from the paper the link between “subjectivity” and these two criteria. This also leads to a question about the argument and the experimental results in Section 6. Section 6 says that subjectivity comes from the conflict between diversity and importance; however, I think diversity is more objective (but still selection of frames is arbitrary), while importance is the main cause of subjectivity. For example, some people may think that a presidential campaign is not important. The paper should provide a convincing discussion on this point. Moreover, I don’t see why the experiments in Section 6 can evaluate diversity and importance. Some quantitative justification is necessary. 

Some recent video summarization papers use multiple training strategies like canonical, augmented, and transfer [Zhang et al, “Video summarization with long short-term memory,” ECCV 2016] and uses more evaluation metrics in [Otani et al, “Rethinking the evaluation of video summaries,” CVPR 2019]. The latter seems important for this paper as it evaluates the scores themselves but not selected frames. The paper will be better if it comes with these different experimental settings and evaluation metrics. 

**Some minor points**

“Semantic gap” is used in a different sense (e.g., [Smeulders et al., "Content-based image retrieval at the end of the early years". IEEE TPAMI, 2000]). This usage may look a little bit confusing. 

The method uses two different techniques to identify event boundaries and shot boundaries, but if they are applied to a video independently, the shot boundaries do not necessarily coincide with some shot boundaries. Some more details on this will be helpful. 

In the ablation study about the effect of semantic hierarchy, more details about the experiments will be helpful (e.g., how $P^{(i)}$ is set when ablating a certain level).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the paper is clearly written and easy to understand, though some details are under-explained. The method itself can be easily reproduced but to reproduce the experimental results, some more details of the data (or publishing the code to generate the data) is necessary. The method in the paper looks novel, but I think it is not entirely justified.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper raises an important question regarding video summarization, but the instantiation is not well motivated nor explained. The hypothesis that subjectivity involves diversity and importance is controversial and is not very convincing nor experimentally validated. Based on these points, I rate the paper negatively.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper mainly deals with three problems in video summarization: 
1. How to understand the storytelling structure of videos. The authors propose a lhierarchical model for video summarization (HiSum), which decomposes videos into event-shot-frame levels and then captures semantic information from top to bottom for understanding video content. 
2. How to evaluate the subjectivity of a video summarization model. In order to evaluate the ability of the model in capturing the diversity and importance, the authors reconstruct the public datasets by means of stitching video clips of different durations. 
3. The recent methods do not use a set-aside validation set for model selection. To address this issue, the authors reset the standard benchmarks for video summarization by correcting the prevalent overfitting issue on the test set. From extensive experiments under a fair setting, HiSum achieves the state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The overall framework looks reasonable and effective.
2. The proposed method outperforms previous methods.
3. The authors provide a new idea for dealing with the subjectivity of video summarization.

Weaknesses：
1. There lacks a visual experiment to illustrate the impact of different granular semantic features on generating summaries.
2. More details are needed to clarify how the authors measure the subjectivity. For example, how labels are generated, and how summaries are generated for synthetic videos.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. In the text summarization field, many methods, e.g., [1, 2], use semantic trees to aggregate information, did the authors refer to relevant literatures?
2. The authors did not describe in detail how the labels of the three datasets (DB, DU, IU) are reconstructed.
3. How the summary ratios are arranged on the reconstructed datasets? 
4. Why is it that splicing video clips of different lengths can model diversity and importance?
5. The authors did not dig deep into the relationship between semantic structure and subjectivity.
6. In Table 3, is there any similarity in model structures between compared methods and the proposed method? It is recommended to compare models with similar structures, e.g., [3], to better prove the superiority of the proposed method.

[1] Wang, Danqing, et al. "Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks for Extractive Document Summarization." Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. 2020.

[2] Sahu, Sunil Kumar, et al. "Inter-sentence Relation Extraction with Document-level Graph Convolutional Neural Network." Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. 2019.

[3] Yao, Ming, et al. "Multi-Level Spatiotemporal Network for Video Summarization." ACM International Conference on Multimedia. 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies video summarization, which is a long-standing problem. To tackle the difficulties in complex structure and subjective goals, it proposes a Hierarchical model for video Summarization (HiSum) to discover the semantic hierarchy structure of a video by event boundary detection. Extensive experiments on two standard benchmarks and three other new datasets demonstrate that the model achieves state-of-the-art performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The paper shows its approach in detail, and the structure is formal.
- The experiments are tested on different datasets. I appreciate the section of different metrics to tackle subjectivity. 

Weaknesses: But I have the following significant concerns on evaluation quality, and novelty:
- The novelty of this paper is questionable. The hierarchy structure of videos is not new, which is studied in existing literature related to movie study, and plot understanding. The criteria of diversity and importance for video summarization are also long-standing in existing works. And it still requires some assumption for these criteria to work. For example, in the case of advertisements, ads are always diverse. Shall we put that into the summary? The authors may need to clarify it. And still, we need to notice that the hour-long TV examples authors shown can not be verified with the TVSum and SumMe datasets.

- The evaluation on TVSum and SumMe is not convincing. They are very old and small datasets that do not satisfy present requirements, where we face tons of videos in different formats every day. The baselines chosen in this paper are weak. The authors are suggested to compare with [1,2].

[1] TL; DW? Summarizing Instructional Videos with Task Relevance & Cross-Modal Saliency. Narasimhan, M., Nagrani, A., Sun, C., Rubinstein, M., Darrell, T., Rohrbach, A. and Schmid, C., ECCV 2022.
[2] CLIP-It! language-guided video summarization. Narasimhan, M., Rohrbach, A. and Darrell, T. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2021.


Minor Typo and Grammar:
“First difficulty is coming” → “The first difficulty comes”
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please refer to the above for clarity, quality, and novelty. For reproducibility, I think a graduate student can reproduce it.
content.summary_of_the_review: Considering the less convincing evaulation and limited novelty of this paper, I think it does not reach the bar of the top-tier ICLR conference and vote for rejection.

content.title: On the Difficulties of Video Summarization: Structure and Subjectivity
content.TL;DR: We tackle subjectivity of video summarization by a semantic boundary-aware hierarchical video modeling.
content.abstract: Video summarization, aiming at selecting a representative set of frames from a video in a limited budget, is a challenging problem in computer vision. First, to summarize a video with complex contents, understanding the storytelling structure is essential, but this fundamental step is still largely under-utilized. Also, summarization is in nature subjective, since each annotator may have different views on what the most important part is within a video. To tackle these difficulties, we propose Hierarchical model for video Summarization (HiSum), discovering semantic hierarchy structure of a video by event boundary detection and taking advantage of it for important frame selection. From extensive experiments on two standard benchmarks and three other new datasets specially designed to take part in subjectivity, we demonstrate that our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance.
